page6_img_1.png.title: Bubble heat map of inter-category influence on application reliability
page6_img_1.png.description: This matrix visualizes how application categories (rows) influence the reliability of other categories (columns): each cell is a pie whose area encodes strength (fraction of target apps affected) and whose orange/blue slices show the fraction of those effects that are positive (increase reliability) or negative (decrease reliability). Rows read as the source of influence and columns as the target; for example the Files and Games rows are dominated by blue pies, indicating these categories mostly correlate with decreased reliability of other apps (the paper reports Files total strength 8.1% and total positivity 14.3%). By contrast, the Security row contains large orange pies (notably Security→Security has the largest strength ≈30.9% and high positivity ≈85.3%), showing many security applications tend to improve the reliability of other security apps, even though the Security column itself is largely blue — meaning security applications are often negatively impacted by non-security categories. Other notable patterns visible are Photo having negative influence on Office and Games but positive on Media, and Office showing a modest overall positive effect on other categories.

page8_img_1.png.title: Bubble matrix of installation-only category influences on application reliability
page8_img_1.png.description: A matrix of pie/bubble glyphs showing how installing (but not frequently using) apps from one category relates to reliability of apps in each target category. Each cell is a pie: the disk size encodes strength (how many target apps are affected) and the orange vs. blue slice encodes positivity (orange = proportion of positive correlations, blue = proportion of negative correlations). The chart shows that, for installation-only cases, Office, Internet and Security rows tend to have large orange pies (mostly positive influence), whereas Files, Photo and Games rows contain several blue pies indicating those installations alone are often associated with decreased reliability of other categories; the rightmost “Total” column summarizes these aggregate trends.

page7_img_table_1.png.title: Security applications' strength and positivity of influence on other apps' reliability
page7_img_table_1.png.description: The table lists 11 anonymized security applications and, for each, two percentages: Strength (the share of the 53 studied applications whose reliability is significantly influenced by that security product) and Positivity (the percentage of those influences that are positive, i.e., associated with increased reliability). Several security products (Security-1, -2, -3, -5, -8 and -10) show only positive influences (100% positivity) with strengths ranging from 1.9% to 13.5%; Security-11 has substantial reach (25.0% strength) and mostly positive effects (84.6% positivity). In contrast, Security-7 stands out as the most influential (36.5% strength) but predominantly harmful, with only 26.3% of its effects being positive. Overall, most security applications in this sample tend to improve other applications’ reliability, though a few exhibit mixed or largely negative impacts.

page8_img_2.png.title: Bubble matrix of category-to-category influences for frequent application usage
page8_img_2.png.description: A matrix of pie-sized bubbles comparing how frequent usage of apps in one category (rows: Internet, Files, Office, Photo, Security, Games, Media, Total) influences reliability of apps in each category (columns). Bubble area encodes strength (how many target apps are affected) and the orange/blue pie slices show positivity: orange = increases reliability, blue = decreases it. The chart shows frequent usage of Files and Games is largely associated with negative effects on many other categories (large blue bubbles, e.g., Files has low positivity overall — total strength 8.1% with only 14.3% positive), whereas Security apps mainly improve reliability (notably a large orange Security→Security bubble; security’s overall strength 12.8% and positivity 71.2%, and Security→Security strength 30.9% with 85.3% positive). Office apps have mixed effects (roughly balanced orange/blue in several cells), and the Total column at the right indicates the net influence of each category, showing that frequent use tends to produce more negative (blue) than positive influences overall, supporting the paper’s finding that heavier usage amplifies negative impacts on other applications.

page5_img_1.png.title: Network of strongest application-to-application influence coefficients
page5_img_1.png.description: A directed influence network of anonymized applications (nodes labeled Internet-#, Media-#, Security-#, Files-#, Office-#, Games-#) where edges show regression coefficients from logistic models: solid orange arrows are strong positive coefficients (presence associated with increased reliability of the target) and dashed blue arrows are strong negative coefficients (presence associated with decreased reliability). Edge labels are the coefficient values: examples visible include Security-9 → Internet-4 (+1.21), Media-12 → Office-5 (+1.59), Security-2 → Internet-1 (+2.13), and Security-7 → Security-11 (+1.67); strong negative links include Internet-12 → Internet-10 (−3.65, an odds-ratio ≈ 1/38) and Media-12 → Media-7 (−1.64). The diagram highlights a cluster of security and Internet nodes with many large positive outgoing effects on other apps, while a smaller set of Internet/Media nodes exert a few large negative influences on particular targets.
